title: Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2017 Measures No. 1) Bill 2017
short_title: Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2017 Measures No. 1) Bill 2017

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would implement further recommendations from a review of medicines and medical devices regulation, including creating a faster approval pathway for certain new medicines.
It would allow provisional marketing approval for promising prescription medicines based on early clinical data, with a two-year registration period that can be extended twice.

The bill would also require sponsors of listed complementary medicines to only use pre-approved indications, and would establish a new assessment pathway for intermediate-risk complementary medicines.
changes: Creates a new class of provisionally registered goods on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods.
Requires sponsors of listed complementary medicines to certify that each indication is on a permitted list set by the Minister.
Establishes an additional assessment pathway for intermediate-risk complementary medicines that seek indications outside the permitted list.
Strengthens post-market monitoring powers for biologicals, including adding record-keeping to standard conditions.
Allows sponsors of listed complementary medicines that have undergone efficacy assessment to indicate this on promotional materials and labels.
Broadens investigation and enforcement powers under the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989.
summary.affected: Sponsors of prescription medicines and complementary medicines, the Department of Health through the Therapeutic Goods Administration, and the Secretary of the Department of Health.

speeches.speaker: Greg Hunt
speeches.brief: The Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2017 Measures No. 1) Bill 2017 was introduced to establish a provisional approval pathway for promising new prescription medicines, allowing patients with unmet clinical needs access up to two years earlier, alongside reforms for medical device approvals, streamlined advertising with a TGA-managed complaint system, stronger compliance powers, and a permitted-indications list for complementary medicines.

speeches.speaker: Greg Hunt
speeches.brief: The bill amends the Therapeutic Goods Act to require Australian corporations designated as conformity assessment bodies to pay an annual charge, enabling cost recovery for postmarket monitoring of medical devices. It also clarifies that annual charges apply to provisionally registered prescription medicines entered under corresponding state laws.

speeches.speaker: Tony Zappia
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2017 Measures No. 1) Bill and related bill, which implement reforms from the 2015 expert panel review, including provisional registration of new medicines, a new pathway for complementary medicines, and stronger postmarket monitoring. The speaker also cautioned about outsourcing TGA responsibilities and pledged to monitor the changes.

speeches.speaker: Greg Hunt
speeches.brief: The Therapeutic Goods Amendment (2017 Measures No. 1) Bill establishes a provisional approval scheme for promising new medicines up to two years sooner, streamlines advertising and regulation of therapeutic goods, and increases post-market monitoring. The companion Therapeutic Goods (Charges) Amendment Bill 2017 introduces annual charges on sponsors using the new provisional evaluation pathway and on designated Australian conformity assessment bodies for medical devices.
